title: Cookies, sessions and browser storage
description: Distinguish between cookies, session identifiers, and client-side storage options, and learn when each is appropriate for maintaining state.

data.text: HTTP is stateless: each request is independent unless the client or server deliberately stores information about the interaction. Cookies, session IDs, and browser storage mechanisms exist to bridge that gap. Choosing the wrong tool leads to security vulnerabilities, broken logins, or unnecessary bandwidth usage.
Cookies are small text strings stored by the browser and automatically sent with requests to matching domains. They are the oldest and most widely supported state mechanism in web development.

data.title: Cookie attributes you must set
items: Expires or Max-Age: when the cookie should be deleted
Secure: send only over HTTPS
HttpOnly: inaccessible to JavaScript to mitigate XSS
SameSite: controls cross-site sending to mitigate CSRF

data.title: Security defaults
data.text: Always set Secure and HttpOnly on authentication cookies. Without them, cookies can be stolen over HTTP or extracted via JavaScript.

A session is server-side state linked to a client by a session identifier, often stored in a cookie. The cookie itself holds only a random ID; the actual data lives on the server, usually in memory, a database, or a cache.

data.title: Typical session flow
items: User submits login credentials.
Server validates credentials and creates a session record.
Server sends a Set-Cookie header with a session ID.
Browser stores the cookie and sends it with subsequent requests.
Server looks up the session ID to retrieve user state.

data.title: Why sessions are safer than storing data in cookies
data.text: Because sensitive session data stays on the server. Even if a cookie is intercepted, the attacker gets only a random identifier, not the underlying user data.
Modern browsers provide client-side storage APIs that are larger and more flexible than cookies, but they are not automatically sent with HTTP requests.

cards.title: localStorage
cards.description: Persistent key-value storage cleared only by JavaScript or the user.
items: Approximately 5-10 MB per origin
Synchronous API; blocks the main thread
Accessible to any script on the page
Not sent with HTTP requests

cards.title: sessionStorage
cards.description: Similar to localStorage but scoped to a single tab or window.
items: Cleared when the tab or window closes
Not shared across tabs
Good for temporary UI state

cards.title: IndexedDB
cards.description: A full transactional database for structured or large data.
items: Asynchronous and non-blocking
Can store much more than localStorage
More complex API
Ideal for offline-first applications

data.title: Guidelines
items: Use session cookies for authentication and short-lived server state.
Use localStorage for non-sensitive client preferences that must persist.
Use sessionStorage for temporary state like form drafts.
Use IndexedDB for offline caches, large datasets, or rich client applications.
Never store passwords or secrets in client-side storage.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Cookies are automatically sent with requests; storage APIs are not.
Sessions keep sensitive data on the server and expose only a session ID.
HttpOnly and Secure flags are essential for authentication cookies.
localStorage, sessionStorage, and IndexedDB serve different persistence needs.
data.takeaway: State management is a deliberate choice. Cookies and sessions handle authentication and server state; browser storage handles client-side preferences and offline needs.

items.question: What is the difference between cookies and sessions?
items.answer: A session is server-side data. A cookie is a client-side storage mechanism. In practice, sessions usually use cookies to transport the session ID.

items.question: Can I store a JWT in localStorage?
items.answer: You can, but it is vulnerable to XSS attacks. Storing tokens in HttpOnly cookies is generally safer. The best choice depends on your threat model and authentication architecture.

items.question: Does sessionStorage survive page refreshes?
items.answer: Yes. It is cleared only when the tab or window is closed.

data.text: Cookies were invented for server state. Do not force them into roles better served by localStorage or IndexedDB.
